title: 7 Luxury Vehicles From Throughout History That Used 4-Cylinder Engines
raw_summary: Luxury cars can differ massively from one another, but most of us make similar assumptions when describing the term "luxury car." We picture leather seats, 20-plus-inch chrome wheels, full-size silhouettes, and big displacement engines with a lot of cylinders . However, every once in a while, automakers mix things up a little and throw in an ingredient you might not expect. Four-cylinder engines are one such ingredient, and they found themselves in luxury cars from an assortment of automakers, spanning across what is almost the entire history of the automobile so far. We're talking Fiats from the turn of the 20th century, British executive sedans produced by Rover in the late '60s and early '70s, hybridized BMW 5 Series sedans, Range Rover SUVs, and more. What's interesting here is that, for the most part, all of these cars were and are considered successes, with rare exceptions (Facel Vega Facellia, we're looking at you), which suggests luxury car buyers aren't actually all that hung up on the engine under the hood. Without further ado, here are our seven four-cylinder luxury cars, in chronological order.

article_paragraphs: Luxury cars can differ massively from one another, but most of us make similar assumptions when describing the term "luxury car." We picture leather seats, 20-plus-inch chrome wheels, full-size silhouettes, and big displacement engines with a lot of cylinders . However, every once in a while, automakers mix things up a little and throw in an ingredient you might not expect. Four-cylinder engines are one such ingredient, and they found themselves in luxury cars from an assortment of automakers, spanning across what is almost the entire history of the automobile so far.

We're talking Fiats from the turn of the 20th century, British executive sedans produced by Rover in the late '60s and early '70s, hybridized BMW 5 Series sedans, Range Rover SUVs, and more. What's interesting here is that, for the most part, all of these cars were and are considered successes, with rare exceptions (Facel Vega Facellia, we're looking at you), which suggests luxury car buyers aren't actually all that hung up on the engine under the hood. Without further ado, here are our seven four-cylinder luxury cars, in chronological order.

Today, Fiat busies itself with budget-oriented and retro-themed compacts mainly, such as the seemingly evergreen 500, plus its new and immensely cute Panda Grande . Wind the clock back just over 120 years to 1905, though, and Fiat was a very different automaker. It was at this point that it debuted its 60 HP model to rival equivalent models from Mercedes. This thunderously powerful car was powered by a 647-cubic-inch inline-4 with dual-chain drive and a four-speed manual transmission. A 60-horsepower inline-4 might not sound like much at all by today's standards, but in vintage car circles, this Fiat is sometimes considered to be the original supercar.

The Fiat 60 HP had a split personality, designed to be capable both as a road-going vehicle and indeed as a racer, with removable wings and advanced cooling systems. It was also mightily expensive, commanding a $13,500 price tag in 1905, while the sole surviving example also wears a $4,000 coachbuilt touring body.

The craftsmen responsible for the body used only the finest materials available, including aluminum panels, silver solder to cover and hide fastening points, and brass mouldings to disguise the seams of the wooden framework. As for the interior, it was about as luxurious as one could expect for a car of this era, with leather seats and mohair floor mats. Remember, just owning a car in the early 20th century was a mind-boggling luxury, let alone one of this caliber.

There is much that could be said about the Facel Vega Facellia that is wholly negative, but for a car so imposing and bold in design, that seems unfair, so we shall begin with its stronger points. Facel Vega knew how to do style and opulence quite well, and although the Facellia was its entry-level model, this experience is still luxurious. It was poised as an excellent alternative to Mercedes' SL series, or indeed an equally charming Alfa Romeo of the same era. Inside, the expected amenities are all there in the form of leather seats and numerous gauges set into a hand-painted woodgrain-effect dashboard. On the outside, there is plenty of brightwork to enjoy, and the Facellia shares much in common stylistically with its bigger brother, the HK500.

However, what it sadly doesn't share with the HK500 is its hulking great Chrysler V8. Instead, the Facellia sported a notoriously unreliable French unit – a 115-hp 1.6-liter inline-4. It suffered from overheating issues, fragile internals, and troublesome chromed cylinder liners, which resulted in the majority of cars experiencing engine failure within the first six months of ownership. Facel Vega had no choice but to replace these engines free of charge, but those second engines didn't prove much better either. A final resolution came in the form of a genuinely bulletproof Volvo lump, but by this point, the firm's reputation was in the gutter, and the Facellia would ultimately prove a hurdle too high for the automaker.

This is a far more conventional offering than the other two covered so far. It replaced the aging P4 model in 1963, and production continued until 1977, so it was clearly a popular choice. With it, Rover successfully filled a notable gap in the UK's car market, where simple commuter cars generally sat at or below 1.5 liters in displacement, while large luxury models sported 3.0 liters or more. With its 2.0-liter inline-4, the P6 could jump between the two segments, offering a premium executive model that cost less than the larger luxury products.

title: Piastri punished for Lindblad collision
raw_summary: Oscar Piastri has lost his points finish in Formula 1’s Mexican Grand Prix as a punishment for his collision with Arvid Lindblad. The McLaren and Racing Bulls came together at the first corner when Piastri tried to take seventh from Lindblad, firing the Racing Bulls briefly into the air and then into the barriers, while Piastri brought his battered car home seventh still.

article_paragraphs: Oscar Piastri has lost his points finish in Formula 1’s Mexican Grand Prix as a punishment for his collision with Arvid Lindblad.

The McLaren and Racing Bulls came together at the first corner when Piastri tried to take seventh from Lindblad, firing the Racing Bulls briefly into the air and then into the barriers, while Piastri brought his battered car home seventh still.
Both drivers were called to the stewards after the race, where Piastri was given a 10-second time penalty that dropped him to 15th in the final results.
“Car 81 [Piastri] was never fully alongside car 41 [Lindblad] so was not able to claim the right to the corner,” said the stewards’ verdict.
“Through Turn 1, the driver of car 41 defended his position by releasing the brakes, however does not force car 81 off the track, allowing racing room on the outside – which he is not required to do.
“The stewards determined that the collision could have been avoided if the driver of car 81 had moved further to the left after Turn 1, even if this involved leaving the track prior to Turn 2.”
“I tried to go up the inside and then he shut the door very, very late, so I had to avoid him and end up on the outside,” he said.
“So, I tried from there and obviously he pushed me pretty wide, and at that point I knew I wasn’t going to complete the overtake, so I was trying to get out.

raw_title: Can One Tire Really Do It All? 8 All-Weather Tires Compete To Find Out
title: Can One Tire Really Do It All? 8 All-Weather Tires Compete To Find Out
raw_summary: Generally speaking, no one can have it all, and no one thing can do it all. That's just not how life works. And for the longest time, that was true of tires. You basically had to pick summer performance, winter performance, or disappointing so-called "all-seasons." Like with engines, though, tire technology advances, and the latest crop of all-weather tires claims to pretty much be able to do it all. But can a single tire really handle every single situation well? Our friends at Tyre Reviews compared eight of them to find out. The newest tire in the comparison is the Continental SecureContact AW, and when it comes to premium tires, a lot of times the newest one is the best. But is that the case here? Well, Tyre Reviews put it up against Michelin's legendary CrossClimate2, the Goodyear Assurance WeatherReady 2, Bridgestone's WeatherPeak, the Pirelli Cinturato WeatherActive, the Hankook Weatherflex GT, the Falken Aklimate, and the Atturo AZ810. And while this is supposedly a Continental-focused comparison, those of you who keep a sharp eye on Jalopnik's tire coverage will recognize that this is also an important comparison test for the much-improved Bridgestone WeatherPeak .

And while this is supposedly a Continental-focused comparison, those of you who keep a sharp eye on Jalopnik's tire coverage will recognize that this is also an important comparison test for the much-improved Bridgestone WeatherPeak .

Tyre Reviews is a YouTube channel that tests tires, then scores them in a variety of categories, weights each category based on how important it is for the comparison in question, and provides some of the best unbiased tire information on the internet. The U.S. doesn't always get every single tire Tyre Reviews tests, but we definitely get the Continental, as well as the Bridgestone. So how did they do?

In the snow handling test, well, I have some bad news for Continental and Bridgestone fans. The Michelin won. That said, the Continental came in second, and the Bridgestone placed fourth. But there's more to winter performance than snow handling, and the Continental edged out the Michelin in snow traction. There's also more to all-weather tires than winter performance, and Tyre Reviews' tests include handling, braking, and performance tests in wet conditions, as well as dry, and they measure factors like noise and rolling resistance, too.

Unfortunately for the Bridgestone, it just didn't have what it took to win this particular comparison. Or beat any of the other tires in the test. Oh, well. As for the Continental, it actually tied with the Michelin ... in first place. Each tire arrived at its first-place score differently, though, so if you want to see which all-weather tire is best for you, you're going to have to watch the video.

title: Hamilton demands 'serious talks' after latest Leclerc incident
raw_summary: Lewis Hamilton says the Ferrari Formula 1 team needs some "serious talks" behind the scenes after the opening lap incident with Charles Leclerc that he thinks cost his team a Mexican Grand Prix win . Having started from pole position, Hamilton had kept his lead at the start through the opening sequence of corners, despite an initial challenge from his team-mate who had got up to second. However, he came under a fresh attack on the run to Turn 4.

article_paragraphs: Lewis Hamilton says the Ferrari Formula 1 team needs some "serious talks" behind the scenes after the opening lap incident with Charles Leclerc that he thinks cost his team a Mexican Grand Prix win .

Having started from pole position, Hamilton had kept his lead at the start through the opening sequence of corners, despite an initial challenge from his team-mate who had got up to second. However, he came under a fresh attack on the run to Turn 4.
As Leclerc attempted to go around the outside, the pair managed to outbrake themselves.

Leclerc ended up cutting across the grass and rejoining after Turn 5, having moved into the lead, while Hamilton ran wide at the Turn 4 exit and lost momentum – allowing Max Verstappen behind him to get past shortly afterwards.
That incident proved decisive as the five-second penalty that Leclerc picked up dropped him behind Verstappen at their first pitstops.

For the remainder of the race, which included a red flag and safety car restart, Hamilton was unable to find a way past Verstappen as he came home second on a day he felt Ferrari had the pace to do better.
Hamilton repeatedly throughout the race expressed his annoyance about Leclerc only picking up a five-second penalty for what he did.
And after finishing second to Verstappen, he felt the way that the events had cost Ferrari was something that needed to be discussed internally.

article_paragraphs: Toyota has Woodland , Honda has TrailSport , Subaru has Wilderness, and now Mitsubishi is getting into the off-road crossover game with what I feel like is the best suffix of them all: the 2028 Mitsubishi Outlander Diamond Trail Edition.

This will take the compact crossover's dirt prowess beyond that of the existing Trail Edition with a tweaked off-road mode for the all-wheel-drive system, a new "Rock" driving mode, and 18-inch off-road wheels with Nexen Roadian ATX all-terrain tires. That new Rock mode automatically turns on Hill Descent Control, uses brakes to minimize wheel-slip, and, Mitsubishi says, does so faster than it would in other drive modes.

A lot of the appeal of an off-road variant is in the aesthetics, and the Diamond Trail Outlander gets a blacked-out grille, darkened headlights, and redesigned bumpers front and rear, meant to improve approach and departure angles. The approach angle is now 20.5 degrees versus 18.3 with the standard Outlander, while the departure angle goes from 22.2 to 23.1 degrees.

Inside, a new water-repellent gray material can be found on the seats, held together by khaki stitching. The digital instrument cluster features a new page that shows off-road-relevant info like front-wheel steering angle, individual wheel-slip, and what the traction control is doing, while the multi-view camera system that lets you see where you should and shouldn't step can now remain on at speeds of up to 18.6 mph versus 6.2 mph in the regular Outlander.

Worth noting is the fact that Mitsubishi is debuting this car at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas next month, marking the first time Mitsubishi is making an appearance there since 2012 — to illustrate how long ago that was in Mitsu terms, the Evo X was still being made and would go on being sold for another four years. A stock Outlander Diamond Trail Edition will be on display alongside two other examples with increasingly extreme aftermarket off-road parts, and we can already hear that booth attendant unironically uttering the words, "It's amazing what a set of wheels and tires can do for these cars."

That name, though, may just be our favorite part of the whole package. Not only does it conjure up images of difficult ski hills, but diamonds actually mean something in the context of this particular brand. In Japanese, "mitsubishi" literally translates to three diamonds, as in the three diamonds that make up its logo. When it entered into a joint venture with Chrysler in 1985, that company was called Diamond-Star Motors (DSM). Mitsubishi once sold a car called the Diamante, and its in-house soccer team is called the Urawa Red Diamonds.

In other words, "Diamond Trail" is very much a Mitsubishi thing, and unlike, say, Nissan's Rock Creek , it isn't just two random outdoorsy words slapped together by some marketing people who thought they'd sound fine together. Diamond Trail also just sounds fun. Just self-serious enough, admittedly a little goofy, and very much imbuing the energy of a brand that — we say this with love — has little to lose.

In any case, Mitsubishi seemingly isn't done making Diamond Trail cars because it says this Outlander "will head a new generation of off-road-capable vehicles." As of right now, Mitsubishi only offers three other models in the U.S. that aren't the Outlander: the smaller Eclipse Cross crossover, the even smaller Outlander Sport crossover, and the Eclipse Sportback EV that's basically a rebadged Nissan Leaf . Hey, Mitsubishi, you know what'd be real cool? A Diamond Trail Edition of that cool new Pajero .

article_paragraphs: The Karma Eximius 1 is the first of nine one-offs featuring extensive styling and mechanical modifications

Karma Automotive has announced a new ultra-exclusive bespoke vehicle program, allowing nine special clients to create an equal number of one-offs with unique styling and mechanical modifications. The first member of the family is a track-focused model dubbed Eximius 1, featuring aggressive aero and a hybrid V8 powertrain.

The Eximius 1 looks like a beefed-up version of the Gyesera . The latter is the successor of the discontinued Revero, itself an evolution of the original Fisker Karma from 2011. The greenhouse, roofline, lights, and doors of the one-off are carried over from the donor vehicle, but everything else has changed.

The aggressive bodykit includes new front and rear bumpers with futuristic intakes and outlets, flanked by diagonal DRLs. These are joined by a vented hood, carbon fiber fender extensions, wider side skirts with aerodynamic fins, a complex diffuser, and a fixed rear spoiler. The body is painted in Borealis Blue with white graphics and exposed carbon fiber bits.

Inside, we find four Recaro bucket seats, Alcantara upholstery painted in Borealis Blue and Moondust, plus a generous amount of carbon fiber. There is also a motorsport-inspired emergency kill switch on the center console, and a custom carbon racing helmet mounted between the rear seats.

While the Gyesera has recently transitioned from a fully electric to a range-extender setup producing a combined 566 hp (422 kW / 574 PS), the Eximius 1 gets something more special. The model is powered by a series plug-in hybrid system centered around a 6.2-liter V8 engine which sounds like its coming from General Motors.

According to Karma, the powertrain has a combined output of around 1,200 hp, with 550 hp coming from the ICE and 650 hp from the electric motors. All this power allows the track-hungry four-seater to accelerate from 0-60 mph (0-96 km/h) in 2.7 seconds, before reaching a top speed of over 200 mph (322 km/h).

The one-off is presumably based on the aluminum spaceframe chassis that dates back to the Fisker days . Still, it benefits from a number of handling-focused modifications including a semi-active suspension by Öhlins, wider tracks, and carbon-ceramic brakes with two-piece slotted brake rotors behind the 21-inch magnesium wheels.

title: Boeing Once Developed A Vehicle For The Navy Called, Adorably, 'Phantom Badger
raw_summary: Sometimes, people will give serious things unserious names. A velvet ant, for example, may sound like a tiny critter that's covered in the sort of material you'd find in an old Land Rover's interior, but it actually has one of the most painful stings in the animal kingdom. Then there's the panhandle hooker: though it sounds like a questionably frisky profession, it actually refers to a dangerous storm that develops in the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma. Or how about the Phantom Badger? We'd have thought it was a mischievous weasel that has a mask-like face, but no. It's actually the name of a military vehicle that was built by Boeing, in partnership with MSI Defense Solutions, starting in 2013. The Phantom Badger was designed to assist U.S. Marine and Air Force squads with a variety of tasks, including, but not limited to, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance missions, and search and rescue.

This versatility is owed to its modular rear section, which allows the Phantom Badger to be quickly repurposed for different roles. It was also built to be easily transported in a Bell-Boeing V-22 Osprey, which is a popular aircraft used by the military.

The Phantom Badger's unclear fate makes exploring its specs even more interesting. While the Navy certified that the Phantom Badger could be transported inside a V-22, the vehicle was not selected for the U.S. Special Operations Command contract it was designed for. Records appear to show no evidence of the Phantom Badger being mass-produced for widespread military service.

As you might be led to believe, the Phantom Badger isn't powered by earthworms and vegetation. Instead, it uses a 3.0-liter multi-fuel V6 turbocharged engine producing up to 240 horsepower and 420 pound-feet of torque. Though we don't really know its 0-60 mph time, we can confirm it hit a maximum of 80 mph on paved surfaces. Its fuel tank is also big enough to provide around 450 miles of range, returning an estimated fuel economy of 21 miles per gallon.

In truth, those are respectable figures. Obviously, it's not quite as fast as a Ford GT Mk IV, the fastest American car to lap the Nürburgring , nor as comfortable as the Rolls-Royce Spectre Series II . But can either of those skip through waters up to three feet deep? We think not. Thanks to the Phantom Badger's height-adjustable suspension and 35-inch tires, not even a mountain of badgers wearing actual phantom masks could stop it.

It is both shorter than a Tesla Model S (180 inches versus 197 inches) and narrower (60 inches versus 86 inches). Now, we're not saying this thing will handle like an Integra R-swapped, left-hand drive Series 1 Lotus Elise , but its turning radius is solid at 24 feet. Staying true to its military makings, it weighs in at a beastly 7,850 pounds and boasts a 3,356-pound maximum payload.

The Phantom Badger has room for five soldiers: two at the front, two at the rear, and one in the middle. Plus, since it's an open-top vehicle, passengers aren't lacking headroom. Let's not forget that the Phantom Badger can hold a 12.7mm machine gun or a 40mm grenade launcher on its weapon mount. The rear hull sits between a pair of swivel stations too, so there are extra places for machine guns up to 7.62mm. Could the infamous honey badger have met its match with the Phantom Badger?

article_paragraphs: Many celebrities and cultural icons claim to love cars and their engineering, but they don't know the first thing about either. McQueen, though, was different.

Dubbed the "King of Cool," McQueen was a hugely talented presence on-screen and unquestionably suave off it. He also had a genuine appreciation for cars and motorcycles. McQueen competed in various levels of motorsport throughout his years and was once even a road tester for Sports Illustrated. As you can imagine, his personal garage was pretty insane, with five vehicles selling for over $1 million at major auction houses.

One of McQueen's cars, his old Ferrari 275 GTB/4*S NART Spider, is heading to auction at Gooding Christie's upcoming New York event, which takes place from November 20 to 21 at the Javits Center in Midtown Manhattan. The Spider is projected to sell for anywhere between $15 million and $20 million, which actually isn't so insane considering the most expensive car ever sold at $143 million .

Ferrari built 10 examples of the NART Spider, and this car, number six, is one of only two finished in 'Blu Sera' (Evening Blue). McQueen purchased it sometime in 1967 and made several modifications soon after, including a darker metallic blue paint finish and reupholstered seat patterns. He also added a smaller motorsport-esque rearview mirror and a quick-fill gas cap, among other things.

It was already a true one-of-one car, but following an accident along the Pacific Coast Highway, which badly damaged the front and rear, McQueen saw further opportunity to customize. He took the car to famed automotive restorer and master painter, Hershel Conway of Junior's House of Color, who flared the fenders a little further and added the 'flip tail' upward-facing rear spoiler.

Oh, and if you're wondering about performance at this point, this diminutive drop-top beauty has around 300 hp in stock form courtesy of a 3.3-liter V12. That's the Ferrari 'Colombo' V12, to be specific, which is considered by many as one of the best engines of all time . If you get the changes right on the five-speed manual shifter, you'll hit 60 mph in just 6.7 seconds and pass a quarter-mile in 14.7 seconds. Remember: this car is almost six decades old.

McQueen sold the Spider in 1971 to designer, inventor, machinist, and amateur racer J. David Kopf, who sold it to NYC's Ferrari specialist, Grand Prix SSR, in 1985. There, the team reverted the Spider to its original Blu Sera paint and completed any other vital work necessary before it found a new home with collector and tech businessman Anthony Wang. It has been with him ever since, and is believed to have only been showcased twice — once in 1996, and another time in 2003.

This car has reached mythical status, given its rarity, history, and condition. We fully expect it to reach the estimated auction price, and then some. McQueen's Porsche 917K from "Le Mans" was previously sold for ... a lot of money, as did the 1926 Excelsior Super X motorcycle he used to ride around his ranch . So, what's stopping this one from landing an eye-watering hammer price? After all, who doesn't want such a significant piece of automotive history floating around their home?

title: Corvette Skidpad Grip Ranked Best To Worst Across Generations
raw_summary: The Chevrolet Corvette has been Detroit's answer to the European sports car for more than seventy years. Since 1953, it has gone through eight distinct generations. The idea behind the Corvette came from Harley Earl, former head of design at General Motors, who envisioned an affordable two-seat roadster that could stand beside the imports returning stateside with World War II veterans. The first Corvette shipped with a six-cylinder engine, and it was Zora Arkus-Duntov (later nicknamed the " Father of the Corvette ") who pushed the car towards the V8 power it would become known for. From there, the Corvette never stopped evolving. The front-engine layout that defined the nameplate for decades was finally abandoned when the eighth generation arrived with its engine behind the driver, a change that purists argued about — and the stopwatch quietly settled. What makes the Corvette so interesting is that it has always been judged by two audiences. One cares about straight-line muscle and badge pride. The other, which is usually more critical, cares about how a car handles when the road bends. And for a car built to take on Porsche, Jaguar, and Ferrari, that second audience matters just as much as the first — if not more.

article_paragraphs: The Chevrolet Corvette has been Detroit's answer to the European sports car for more than seventy years. Since 1953, it has gone through eight distinct generations. The idea behind the Corvette came from Harley Earl, former head of design at General Motors, who envisioned an affordable two-seat roadster that could stand beside the imports returning stateside with World War II veterans. The first Corvette shipped with a six-cylinder engine, and it was Zora Arkus-Duntov (later nicknamed the " Father of the Corvette ") who pushed the car towards the V8 power it would become known for.

From there, the Corvette never stopped evolving. The front-engine layout that defined the nameplate for decades was finally abandoned when the eighth generation arrived with its engine behind the driver, a change that purists argued about — and the stopwatch quietly settled. What makes the Corvette so interesting is that it has always been judged by two audiences. One cares about straight-line muscle and badge pride. The other, which is usually more critical, cares about how a car handles when the road bends. And for a car built to take on Porsche, Jaguar, and Ferrari, that second audience matters just as much as the first — if not more.

That is where skidpad grip comes in. Measured in g-force, it shows how hard a car can corner before the tires let go of the road. This measurement largely sidesteps horsepower and driver skill (as you'll see throughout this article), instead mostly being affected by tires, suspension, and chassis balance. To keep the numbers easier to digest, this article leans on Car and Driver 's skidpad, which is 300 feet across in its modern tests and 200 feet in older ones. Other testers will be relied on only where necessary.

In terms of available and credible test results online, the C7 is where the front-engine Corvette actually peaked. On Car and Driver's 300-foot skidpad, the 2015 Z06 with the Z07 package "scorched the skidpad with 1.19 g." At the time, no production car had logged a higher figure on that pad. The Z06 also managed to stop in 128 feet from 70 mph to 0, cross the quarter mile in just 11 seconds at 126 mph, and do a 0 to 60 mph run in just 2.9 seconds.

Behind that number sat a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 rated at 650 horsepower, as well as Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 ZP tires. Weight-wise, the car itself is rated at 3,558 pounds. Car and Driver also posted impressive numbers with the 2017 Corvette Grand Sport, which managed to hold 1.18 g even with 190 fewer horsepower than the Z06, showing how engine strength doesn't matter as much as other factors for grip. Braking from 70 mph took 129 feet, the quarter-mile took 12.2 seconds, and 60 mph arrived in 3.8 seconds. And the Grand Sport is only slightly lighter than the Z06, tipping the scales at 3,452 pounds.

Interestingly, the Z06's 1.19 g is also higher than anything the C8 posted in Car and Driver's tests. Even the 1,064-horsepower 2025 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 managed a curiously low 1.13 g. In other words, the C7 Z06's 1.19 g is a measurement that no other Corvette generation could match.

The mid-engine C8 had every reason to beat the C7 here. It is the newer car, it has the newer rubber, and it has more horsepower across the board. The Z06's 5.5-liter flat-plane-crank V8 makes 670 horsepower, and the Z07 package has the car riding on Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 R tires. But on Car and Driver 's 300-foot skidpad, the Z07-equipped Z06 recorded 1.16 g. Chevrolet's own number for the car was 1.22 g, and Car and Driver noted that this result was "well below the company's estimate." The publication later explained that the Z07's tires had been inflated to the door-placard pressure rather than Chevrolet's lower track recommendation, potentially limiting its measured grip.

Regardless, even if we look at the rest of the lineup, the C8 failed to match the C7 in Car and Driver's tests. The non-Z07 version of the Z06 convertible hit 1.12 g, and the Stingray reached just 1.03 g. Later Car and Driver tests didn't move the number; as mentioned, the ZR1 reached 1.13 g, while the 1,250-horsepower ZR1X came in at 1.15 g. That leaves the C8 0.03 g behind the C7 Z06's result in Car and Driver's testing.

title: FIA explains controversial Leclerc penalty decision
raw_summary: The FIA Formula 1 stewards have explained why Charles Leclerc was only given a five-second penalty for cutting the track and passing Lewis Hamilton for the lead of the Mexico Grand Prix on the opening lap. The Ferrari team-mates were duelling for the front spot from the start, having already gone side by side through the opening sequence of corners when Leclerc made a move on the outside of Turn 4.
summary: The FIA Formula 1 stewards have explained why Charles Leclerc was only given a five-second penalty for cutting the track and passing Lewis Hamilton for the lead of the Mexico Grand Prix on the opening lap. The Ferrari team-mates were duelling for the front spot from the start, having already gone side by side through the opening sequence of corners when Leclerc made a move on the outside of Turn 4.
article_paragraphs: The FIA Formula 1 stewards have explained why Charles Leclerc was only given a five-second penalty for cutting the track and passing Lewis Hamilton for the lead of the Mexico Grand Prix on the opening lap.
The Ferrari team-mates were duelling for the front spot from the start, having already gone side by side through the opening sequence of corners when Leclerc made a move on the outside of Turn 4.
Both drivers braked as late as possible, with Leclerc running wide and cutting across the grass before rejoining at the front after Turn 5.
Behind him Hamilton, in his attempt to defend by braking late, had run slightly wide - costing him momentum which allowed the pursuing Max Verstappen to make a move and snatch second spot.
This area of the track was, like the first corners, subject to a special rule to avoid shenanigans on opening laps of drivers cutting across the grass to gain positions.

In a note sent to teams ahead of the race, following discussions in the drivers' briefing, the FIA said: "Any car leaving the track in these areas and maintaining a position to a car or cars within close proximity behind (as determined by the stewards) may be considered as gaining a lasting advantage, unless such position is yielded by Turn 4 [in the case of a car leaving the track in the area of Turns 1 to 3], or by Turn 12 [in the case of a car leaving the track in the area of Turns 4 to 6.]”
With Leclerc having not given up the place to Hamilton, he was therefore put under investigation for gaining an advantage – and it was decided that he would get a five-second penalty.

That proved controversial though with Hamilton in particular feeling that, with the advantage that Leclerc gained from having clean air which allowed him to build up a buffer, the sanction should have been the standard 10 seconds.

title: Dodge Entered The US Compact Truck Market Late With A Rebadged Mitsubishi Forte
raw_summary: Heading into the 1960s, Detroit's Big Three had begun to realize some folks preferred cars that were more agile and more efficient than the typically massive machines they were producing. Their response was to introduce a wave of home-grown compacts in 1960, led by GM's Chevrolet Corvair, the Chrysler Valiant, and the Ford Falcon. On the truck side of the ledger, though, things played out differently. Datsun had been exporting compact trucks to the West Coast since the first half of the 1960s, with Toyota following soon after. The Big Three at the time offered car-based trucks like the Corvair forward-control models and the Falcon-based ute-style Ranchero, but they didn't look like the real deal the way the Japanese mini-trucks did. So when the mini-truck segment began taking off, the U.S. automakers went straight to the easiest option. Ford rebadged Mazda's B-series truck to sell as the Courier for 1972. The same year saw GM give that treatment to the Isuzu Faster, with the result being the Chevy LUV — a truck way ahead of its time .

article_paragraphs: Heading into the 1960s, Detroit's Big Three had begun to realize some folks preferred cars that were more agile and more efficient than the typically massive machines they were producing. Their response was to introduce a wave of home-grown compacts in 1960, led by GM's Chevrolet Corvair, the Chrysler Valiant, and the Ford Falcon.

On the truck side of the ledger, though, things played out differently. Datsun had been exporting compact trucks to the West Coast since the first half of the 1960s, with Toyota following soon after. The Big Three at the time offered car-based trucks like the Corvair forward-control models and the Falcon-based ute-style Ranchero, but they didn't look like the real deal the way the Japanese mini-trucks did. So when the mini-truck segment began taking off, the U.S. automakers went straight to the easiest option. Ford rebadged Mazda's B-series truck to sell as the Courier for 1972. The same year saw GM give that treatment to the Isuzu Faster, with the result being the Chevy LUV — a truck way ahead of its time .

As a result, the Courier and LUV, and their Japanese-branded rivals, were in the right place at the right time when the fuel crises of 1970s hit, starting in 1973. Chrysler's entry, though, was way behind. Based on the Mitsubishi Forte, the Dodge D-50 didn't debut until 1979, some seven years after the Courier and LUV. (To be clear, the D-50 would be renamed the Dodge Ram 50 in 1981, and Mitsubishi's Forte is unrelated to Kia's former compact sedan of the same name.)

Unlike today, compact pickups of the past were literally compact. So the 1979 Dodge D-50 pickup had a slightly smaller footprint than a 2026 Honda Civic sedan. The D-50 is 184.6 inches in length and 65 inches wide, while the Civic is 0.2 inches longer and 5.9 inches wider. As for a modern "compact" pickup, the Ford Maverick is 15.2 inches longer, 7.6 inches wider, and 8 inches taller.

The D-50's power train was likewise fairly small. The standard mill was a 2.0-liter overhead-cam inline-4 capable of 93 horsepower and 108 pound-feet of torque, and it was paired with a four-speed manual transmission. For the D-50 Sport, a 2.6-liter I4 with 105 horses and 139 lb-ft was standard with a five-speed automatic with overdrive. A three-speed automatic was optional with both versions.
More impressive was the D-50's maximum payload of 1,400 pounds. By 1981, when the D-50's payload rating reached 1,525 pounds, it could out-carry the '26 Maverick, which has a 1,500-pound payload.

The year 1981 further marked two other milestones for the Dodge. The first was a marketing change. Ram and Dodge aren't the same brand anymore , having split up in 2009, but they were still connected at the time. And in 1981, when Chrysler was readying its new truck lineup for the year, the decision was made to add the Ram name to the roster – transforming its compact into the Dodge Ram 50. The next year saw the Ram 50 welcome its first 4x4 configuration, complete with another new marketing move that positioned the truck as the Power Ram 50. The truck even offered a diesel power plant from 1983 to 1985.

The Dodge Ram 50 would go on to get a second generation in 1987, and that model would remain in production until 1994. Yet not only wasn't it the smallest Dodge pickup ever produced, it wasn't even the smallest Dodge pickup of its era. That honor goes to the Dodge Rampage.

raw_title: What The 'E' On A Manual Gear Shift Means (And When To Use It)
title: What The 'E' On A Manual Gear Shift Means (And When To Use It)
raw_summary: Long before our cars got fancy drive mode selectors, trick cylinder deactivation tech, and varying levels of hybrid assistance , automakers had to get creative with their engineering approach to satisfy the tightening fuel economy standards that arrived during the oil crisis of the late '70s and early '80s. article_paragraphs: Long before our cars got fancy drive mode selectors, trick cylinder deactivation tech, and varying levels of hybrid assistance , automakers had to get creative with their engineering approach to satisfy the tightening fuel economy standards that arrived during the oil crisis of the late '70s and early '80s. Volkswagen's solution was a special manual gearbox design where the final shift gate was marked with a capital 'E'.

The '3+E' and '4+E' setups found in the original VW Golf , Jetta, and the U.S.-spec Rabbit models had nothing to do with electrification. Many drivers at the time understandably assumed that the letter stood for 'Economy' or an 'Extra' gear. However, Volkswagen documents confirm that the magic word is 'Efficiency'. Rather than being a new designation for the fourth or fifth gears, the 'E' slot engaged an overdrive designed to lower engine speeds, minimize wear, and improve the fuel economy ratings at highway speeds.

The concept of overdrive wasn't new. Earlier British and European cars often relied on external electro-hydraulic units like the Laycock de Normanville system, which bolted onto the back of a conventional gearbox and was triggered by a dash switch or column stalk. Volkswagen's approach was different, integrating the tall overdrive ratio directly inside the transaxle's gear casing of its front-wheel-drive platform, and putting control on the manual shift lever. The '3+E' gearbox of the 1981 VW Rabbit LS was effectively a four-speed casing with wider spacing.

First, second, and third gears covered roughly 90% of all urban and B-road driving scenarios, while the 'E' gear was ideal for highway use thanks to its 0.70:1 overdrive ratio, running through a 3.89:1 final drive. While not a fuel economy record-breaking car by modern standards, when slipping the Rabbit into 'E', engine revs dropped to 2,500 rpm at 60 mph, boosting fuel efficiency from 24 mpg on the older four-speed up to 28 mpg, with highway figures reaching 42 mpg. However, this gear was best for holding a certain speed, meaning that drivers had to downshift in order to gain access to the full engine power.

In Europe, Volkswagen went a step further by introducing a special trim known as 'Formula E' (Formel E in German) across its entire lineup between 1981 and 1985. Not to be confused with modern battery-powered Formula E race cars , VW's system was instead focused on improving efficiency. It was available in the Polo, Golf, Jetta, Scirocco, Passat, and Santana, as well as the Audi 80 and 100 of the same era. The '4+E' transmission was combined with subtle aerodynamic tweaks and an early form of driver coaching.

An electro-vacuum computer monitored engine load against RPM and illuminated an amber arrow on the instrument cluster signaling the driver to upshift for optimum efficiency. After 1985, the introduction of electronic multi-point fuel injection, variable valve timing, and standardized five- and six-speed manual transmissions rendered these '3+E' and '4+E' setups obsolete. Engineers found ways to achieve superior real-world fuel economy without compromising drivability or forcing drivers to navigate massive gear gaps.

raw_title: Batteries Beat Norway’s Hydrogen Bulk Carriers on Cost in Two Modeled Routes
title: Batteries Beat Norway's Hydrogen Bulk Carriers on Cost in Two Modeled Routes
raw_summary: Norwegian shipping company GMI Group is moving ahead with four hydrogen-electric bulk carriers for coastal freight. In October 2026, PowerCell confirmed a follow-up order that brings the program to 24 marine fuel-cell units with 5.4 MW of combined installed capacity. The first two ships, rated at 4,000 deadweight tonnes, are planned for 2027, while two additional 3,000-tonne vessels are expected in 2029. The project has real shipbuilding commitments and substantial public support. The question is whether hydrogen makes economic sense for the freight services these vessels will provide.
summary: Norwegian shipping company GMI Group is moving ahead with four hydrogen-electric bulk carriers for coastal freight. In October 2026, PowerCell confirmed a follow-up order that brings the program to 24 marine fuel-cell units with 5.4 MW of combined installed capacity. The first two ships, rated at 4,000 deadweight tonnes, are planned for 2027, while two additional 3,000-tonne vessels are expected in 2029.
article_paragraphs: Norwegian shipping company GMI Group is moving ahead with four hydrogen-electric bulk carriers for coastal freight. In October 2026, PowerCell confirmed a follow-up order that brings the program to 24 marine fuel-cell units with 5.4 MW of combined installed capacity. The first two ships, rated at 4,000 deadweight tonnes, are planned for 2027, while two additional 3,000-tonne vessels are expected in 2029.
The project has real shipbuilding commitments and substantial public support. The question is whether hydrogen makes economic sense for the freight services these vessels will provide.

GMI says its design can deliver lifetime costs 9–10% below conventional ships. Its argument combines fuel cells, batteries, an efficient hull and wind assistance. Those are useful engineering features, but most are not exclusive to hydrogen propulsion. A diesel or battery-electric ship can have a similarly efficient hull and sails. The fuel and energy systems still need to be compared on equivalent terms.

I modeled two hypothetical 3,000-tonne coastal bulk services, covering 80 and 55 nautical miles, using comparable hull performance and operating requirements. Over fifteen years, hydrogen propulsion came out 50–58% more expensive than conventional diesel, even after assuming approximately €13.1 million in public vessel support was received upfront. Battery-electric alternatives were €11.64–14.13 million cheaper than the subsidized hydrogen vessels. These are scenario results, not estimates of GMI’s actual operating contracts.

The company has not published the route and commercial data needed for a direct assessment, and the model’s vessel acquisition prices remain important uncertainties. The battery alternatives were not the cheapest option under every assumption. In the central cases they cost somewhat more than diesel over fifteen years. Their advantage was the much smaller gap to conventional operation compared with hydrogen. Battery-electric propulsion also requires adequate grid connections, charging equipment and berth time, which cannot be assumed available at every Norwegian port.

Hydrogen has a different set of requirements. Renewable electricity must be converted into hydrogen, compressed, stored, delivered to the vessel and converted back to electricity in fuel cells. Those additional processes introduce energy losses and capital costs that efficient hulls and sails cannot erase. They matter particularly for short coastal voyages where a practical charging arrangement may be possible.

Norway is using substantial public funding to support the hydrogen ships. Norsk Hydrogenforum reports Enova awards totaling roughly €42.9 million for the four vessels. Additional public support has been awarded to GreenH hydrogen production projects. Announced grants are not necessarily fully paid, and a subsidy changes the allocation of costs rather than eliminating the equipment and energy required.

There may be coastal services where voyage length, available berth time or grid limitations favour hydrogen over batteries. That needs to be established through engineering and commercial comparisons, rather than inferred from the existence of a funded shipbuilding program.

raw_title: Hackers Figured Out How Flock Camera Systems Actually Work By Pulling One Apart
title: Hackers Figured Out How Flock Camera Systems Actually Work By Pulling One Apart
raw_summary: If you've ever wondered exactly how easy it is to hack Flock cameras , the results are in, and it seems they're pretty darn vulnerable to hacking attempts. For the past couple years, several hacking groups have targeted Flock cameras and other Fourth Amendment-breaking automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and proven their security vulnerabilities time and again. In some cases, Flock cameras have been found to be streaming live and archived video over the open internet, and in others, it took only about 30 seconds to gain access to a camera's stored footage after getting the box open. Another recent hacking attempt has caught the public's attention, revealing the extent of the cameras' so-called encryption (spoiler: it's not good) and showing how much data ALPRs capture daily. The initial report of this hacking attempt — covered together by Wired and 404Media — details how the hackers acquired a Flock camera, cracked open its shell, and made a nearly perfect copy of the data inside.
summary: If you've ever wondered exactly how easy it is to hack Flock cameras , the results are in, and it seems they're pretty darn vulnerable to hacking attempts. For the past couple years, several hacking groups have targeted Flock cameras and other Fourth Amendment-breaking automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and proven their security vulnerabilities time and again.
article_paragraphs: If you've ever wondered exactly how easy it is to hack Flock cameras , the results are in, and it seems they're pretty darn vulnerable to hacking attempts. For the past couple years, several hacking groups have targeted Flock cameras and other Fourth Amendment-breaking automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and proven their security vulnerabilities time and again. In some cases, Flock cameras have been found to be streaming live and archived video over the open internet, and in others, it took only about 30 seconds to gain access to a camera's stored footage after getting the box open.

Another recent hacking attempt has caught the public's attention, revealing the extent of the cameras' so-called encryption (spoiler: it's not good) and showing how much data ALPRs capture daily. The initial report of this hacking attempt — covered together by Wired and 404Media — details how the hackers acquired a Flock camera, cracked open its shell, and made a nearly perfect copy of the data inside.

The hacking collective behind this recent hacking attempt is known as stegan0gram, and the members represent just a small fraction of the people around the United States who keep vandalizing these ALPRs tracking our every move . Stegan0gram is taking things a step further, though. In an interview with 404Media, one of the hackers discussed "liberating" the hardware and reverse engineering it. The anonymous agent laid our their philosophy, asking "Why just destroy them when we can reverse engineer them and find the secrets of those spying on us?"

A good question, indeed, stegan0gram. With cities all over the country ditching the ALPR laughing stock that is Flock Safety in favor of companies like Axon, which collect similar data and give law enforcement agencies unfettered, warrantless access to it, such secrets are well worth uncovering.

Flock cameras and cameras from companies like Axon are called ALPRs, which would imply that what they do is, you know, automatically read license plates. However, the term is something of a misnomer. Despite Flock Safety's claims that their network of over 100,000 spy cameras doesn't track individuals or any information other than a car's "signature," it's been known for some time that these privacy-eroding cameras are capturing more than just plates . The recent hack by sten0gram shows that ALPRs are capable of surveilling the public in much scarier ways.

When the hackers opened up their camera and looked inside, they found some data unencrypted, including a section of the camera's memory bank titled "media," inside which was stored an encryption key that opened up previously encrypted data. In effect, a company that sells your location, driving patterns, and life story to law enforcement, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, hid the key to their house under the welcome mat.

With the newly decrypted data, the hackers had access to records of over 50,000 vehicles, including over 1.5 million images. The camera's highlights also clearly showed that the technology knows how to detect individuals, license plates, and bicycles, in addition to motor vehicles. The collective also found that the camera had logged bumper stickers, license plate frames, and other graphics, likely misidentifying them as plates.

What doesn't seem to happen inside the camera is also notable. From when stegan0gram could determine, Flock cameras don't actually read license plates locally. Nor do they build a car's signature, using data like make, model, color, and identifying features. Instead, these operations are likely done on Flock's own servers after the data is transferred from the camera.

title: Eli teases the launch of a much faster electric microcar
raw_summary: Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane. In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.

article_paragraphs: Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.

In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.
The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.

The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).

A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.
If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.

The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.
It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.

raw_title: Relaunched Mitsubishi Pajero Is Already Stealing Land Cruiser Customers
title: Relaunched Mitsubishi Pajero Is Already Stealing Land Cruiser Customers
raw_summary: It's been less than two months since the Mitsubishi Pajero officially re-entered the off-road-focused SUV scene , and it's already making waves. Long-beleaguered Mitsubishi says that a whopping 80% of the Pajero's customers in Japan are coming from competitors as it looks to move upmarket with a $39,000 base price — primed to challenge the mighty Toyota Land Cruiser. Of course, a great deal of that 80% number makes sense, considering Mitsubishi doesn't really make anything all that compelling right now, and hasn't for some time. Honestly, I'd assume the other 20% of non-conquest buyers are just folks coming from old Pajeros. In any case, Mitsu' unveiled domestic pricing and specs for its new flagship this week, adding that it had already received 5,500 orders in Japan for the Japan-built body-on-frame SUV — 1,500 more than what was expected, according to Automotive News . It puts the seven-seater well on its way to hitting Mitsubishi's goal of 10,000 sales through March of 2027. Sales are officially slated to begin in Japan on December 17, with the Australian market getting theirs the following month. It's already on sale in Thailand, with 1,500 orders so far.

Mitsubishi clearly had its sights set on the Toyota Land Cruiser lineup when designing, engineering and pricing the new Pajero . In Japan, it's priced at the equivalent of $39,212, which places it slightly above the entry point of the Land Cruiser 250 ($36,596) and directly in line with the base-level utilitarian version of the twin-turbo Land Cruiser 300 ($39,890). Volume versions of the LC300 start at a far higher $55,406, according to Automotive News, and they go all the way up to $64,586 for the top-end GR Sport hybrid. Stateside, the only Land Cruiser we get is the smaller 250 , and it starts at $59,775, including destination. If the Pajero/Montero were to come here, I wouldn't be shocked if it were to cost somewhere in that neighborhood.

In any case, Mitsubishi has to be feeling good about what the Pajero is already bringing to the table. That 80% conquest number is nothing to sneeze at, and the company says many former Pajero owners who left the brand when the company dropped the nameplate globally in 2020 are returning, Automotive News reports. Those buyers are also going for big options — ignoring the bargain-basement attitude Mitsubishi has cultivated in the past years. About 70% of Japanese orders are for vehicles equipped with premium packages, which has to be amazing news for a company looking to switch up its image in a major way.

Despite all of this, there's still no word on whether we're going to get our Montero stateside , but by all that's holy, I want it. Mitsubishi says it's evaluating other markets and plans other power trains beyond the current diesel, but I won't hold my breath.

raw_title: Yes, electric motorcycles will replace gasoline motorcycles, but not the way you think
title: Yes, electric motorcycles will replace gasoline motorcycles, but not the way you think
raw_summary: For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch. It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.
summary: For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch. It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.
article_paragraphs: For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch.
It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.

But I think we’ve been looking at electric motorcycles all wrong. Because the future of electric motorcycles isn’t necessarily about convincing today’s gasoline motorcycle riders to switch. It’s about the next generation of riders who won’t have any reason to start with gasoline in the first place.

And that’s a much bigger deal than it might sound. In fact, it’s the entire key to the puzzle. Because make no mistake, the future of motorcycling is electric. It just won’t happen the way most people think.
The problem with applying the electric car playbook to motorcycles is that motorcycles aren’t cars.

For most people, a car is a tool. It’s transportation. Sure, some drivers are deeply passionate about their cars, but they are a minority. The vast majority simply want something comfortable, reliable, affordable, and convenient to get them from point A to point B.

Motorcycles, especially in markets like the US and Europe, are different. In fact, it’s the complete opposite of the car situation. For a minority of Western riders, and especially American riders, a motorcycle is a tool. For the vast majority, it’s a passion. People generally buy motorcycles because they love motorcycles. And for many riders, that love is deeply intertwined with the gasoline engine itself.
The sound, the vibration, the shifting, the mechanical character. These aren’t necessarily flaws to be engineered away. They’re part of the experience for traditional riders.

It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed.
Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.

raw_title: Why Cars And Long Scarves Don't Mix
title: Why Cars And Long Scarves Don't Mix
raw_summary: Cars are dangerous. There's no shortage of studies reiterating that fact, from the frequent running down of pedestrians over the last century to the not-so-obvious deaths outside of traffic crashes . It's why many of today's cars are inundated with those darn safety features we'd sacrifice if given the option. And yet another danger lurks in an unexpected place: the closet. Caution the fashionistas in your life, because your car and a scarf could be a deadly combination. Death by scarf via the automobile became a phenomenon nearly 100 years ago, when in 1927, famous American dancer Isadora Duncan met her tragic end from the combination of the two in France. The New York Times wrote that on the night of the accident, she wore an "immense iridescent silk scarf wrapped about her neck and streaming in long folds, part of which was swathed about her body with part trailing behind."

The story continues that after a walk along the promenade in Nice, she hopped into a rented car and neither she nor the driver had realized one of the ends of her massive scarf had fallen outside of the car. The stray piece caught in the rear wheel and wound around enough that it then pulled Duncan from out of the car where she was dragged behind it for several feet. The driver stopped the car, but it was too late. When aid arrived on scene, they stated she had been killed instantly from strangulation.

Duncan's death became so well-known that similar occurrences were deemed Isadora Duncan syndrome (also referred to as long-scarf syndrome ). These are typically accidental strangulations with trauma injuries sustained to the larynx and trachea (the airway), and potentially the carotid arteries (delicate mainlines of blood to the brain). Damage to either of these throughways for vital resources could starve the brain of oxygen and lead to death, like it tragically did for Duncan.

Scarf-induced deaths do still happen in modern times , and they're more likely to happen when the mode of transportation is wide open to the elements — something like an auto-rickshaw or a convertible is a dangerous place to wear a long scarf. The prevalence of modern scarf incidents actually inspired an Indian study which specifically looked at scarf deaths from 2013 to 2015 within a Level 1 trauma center. Over the nearly two years the study was conducted, 76 injuries were recorded, and approximately three of those individuals died from related injuries.

Other recent instances outside of India include two women who were maimed by scarves worn for special occasions just this month. The first, a Dallas woman , opted to wear a long dress with a scarf to a wedding. Post-wedding, with friends, they got into a car to go to dinner. Her scarf became stuck in the door, and trailed off enough to get caught in the tire. It pulled on her neck hard enough to cause a nasty friction burn across the lower part of her neck and shoulder.

A video account of the Dallas event was stitched by another woman who also had a physically scarring scarf experience . She shared that she too had been "nearly killed by fashion" when she wore the scarf part of her newly purchased dress for a gala. Caught in the seatbelt and the door of a rideshare vehicle, the woman's scarf was eventually pulled by the tire, which led to an eventual trip to the emergency room.

Both women were somewhat lucky to have only suffered deep burns to their neck and not more serious injuries, or death like Duncan. The lesson here: If you're going to wear a scarf, be vigilant about where that scarf is when you get into a vehicle.

title: Are Kia And Hyundai's Engines The Same?
raw_summary: The relationship between Hyundai and Kia today is not what it was like in the past. Kia was founded in 1944, while Hyundai was formed in 1967. It was only after Kia declared bankruptcy in 1997 that its South Korean rival stepped in and bought a 51% stake. Now, Kia and Hyundai are like two peas in a pod, sharing technologies, architectures, and engines. A slew of engines are shared between Hyundai and Kia. One notable example is the turbodiesel 2.2-liter CRDi inline-4 that's been available in the Hyundai Santa Fe and Kia Sorento since 2009. It's built at Hyundai's factory in South Korea and is generally regarded as a solid, reliable engine, though issues with the piezo-electronic injectors can cause it to run poorly and necessitate expensive repairs. The 2.2-liter CRDi is also known to sometimes suffer from high oil consumption, potentially sipping up to 0.5 liters per 600 miles. Beyond the Santa Fe and Sorento, this engine is also found in the Hyundai Palisade, Hyundai Sonata, and Kia Carnival.

article_paragraphs: The relationship between Hyundai and Kia today is not what it was like in the past. Kia was founded in 1944, while Hyundai was formed in 1967. It was only after Kia declared bankruptcy in 1997 that its South Korean rival stepped in and bought a 51% stake. Now, Kia and Hyundai are like two peas in a pod, sharing technologies, architectures, and engines.

A slew of engines are shared between Hyundai and Kia. One notable example is the turbodiesel 2.2-liter CRDi inline-4 that's been available in the Hyundai Santa Fe and Kia Sorento since 2009. It's built at Hyundai's factory in South Korea and is generally regarded as a solid, reliable engine, though issues with the piezo-electronic injectors can cause it to run poorly and necessitate expensive repairs. The 2.2-liter CRDi is also known to sometimes suffer from high oil consumption, potentially sipping up to 0.5 liters per 600 miles. Beyond the Santa Fe and Sorento, this engine is also found in the Hyundai Palisade, Hyundai Sonata, and Kia Carnival.

Another noteworthy engine used across several Hyundai and Kia models is the Smartstream turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4, sold in the likes of the Santa Fe, Sonata, and K5, though it's mostly found in Asian markets. Related to this engine is the Smartstream turbocharged 2.5-liter inline-4. It powers the Hyundai Sonata N Line, Kia Sorento, and several Genesis models. According to reports, this engine may also power the next-generation Hyundai N cars .

The two brands share a turbocharged 3.5-liter V6, known as the Smartstream G3.5, while Hyundai also builds a twin-turbo version for the Genesis brand. Sharing engines makes sense for the companies, as they can split development and manufacturing costs without the need to establish dedicated supply chains. Many of these shared Hyundai engines are manufactured right here in the United States . The list includes the Smartstream G2.5GDi and T-GDi engines, as well as the G1.6 T-GDi, and G2.0 Atkinson.

If you buy a Hyundai or Kia model, such as the Kia Telluride or Sportage, or perhaps a Hyundai Tucson, Santa Cruz, or Santa Fe built in the U.S., there's a good chance it'll have a homegrown engine. For the most part, American buyers can rest easy knowing their new Hyundai or Kia should have a reliable engine, and if something does go wrong, all are covered by a standard 10-year/100,000-mile warranty. While most engines the brand currently uses are solid, some have had issues in the past.

Two of the most notable engines with issues are the 1.8-liter and 2.0-liter inline-4 Nu mills, and the 1.8-liter, 2.0-liter, and 2.4-liter Theta II inline-4 units. These engines have been the subject of several recalls and a large class-action lawsuit with Kia and Hyundai in the United States over reports that they can stall, seize, and catch fire. In 2024, the automakers agreed to settle the lawsuit, providing cash rebates for affected owners and extending engine warranties to 15 years or 150,000 miles.

The downside of engine sharing between Hyundai and Kia is that if an engine family has issues, several vehicles from both brands are likely to be affected. In this case, the Nu and Theta II issues impacted models included the 2011-2015 Hyundai Sonata Hybrid and 2014-2021 Hyundai Tucson, along with the 2011-2016 Kia Optima Hybrid and 2011-2013 Kia Sportage models, among others. It's worth noting that the parts sharing between Hyundai and Kia extends beyond the engines.

Many EVs built by the two brands also share components. This includes the Kia EV6, Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9, and Genesis GV60 — all of which use the 800-volt E-GMP platform with shared battery packs and electric motors. The Hyundai Ioniq 3 and Kia EV4 use a 400-volt version of this architecture.

title: Peterbilt makes it easier than ever for government fleets to go electric
raw_summary: Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell. The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5- 8 commercial trucks . That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.

article_paragraphs: Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell.

The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5- 8 commercial trucks . That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.

“Our long-standing relationship with Sourcewell reflects Peterbilt’s commitment to delivering solutions tailored to the unique needs of public fleets,” explains Erik Johnson, assistant general manager of sales and marketing at Peterbilt . “By adding our electric vehicles to the contract and eliminating lengthy bidding processes, we’re helping organizations maximize uptime and invest their resources where it matters most, keeping their communities running.”
I hear some of you asking, “Why is this important, and what exactly is Sourcewell?” And you’re very smart to ask.

See, when your state or local government decides it needs a new truck, it can’t just call up someone’s cousin and cut an inflated check backed by your tax dollars ( regardless of what you saw on Fox News ). Instead, public agencies generally have to follow competitive purchasing rules that are designed to ensure fairness, transparency, and responsible use of taxpayer money. That can mean writing and publishing a request for proposals (RFP), publicly soliciting bids, evaluating competing offers, and even allowing public comments that can all-too easily devolve into 17 hours of Pawnee-level discourse among stakeholders (real and imagined) about the relative merits of competing proposals.

Sourcewell is a government agency that basically does all that ahead of time , publishing RFPs, soliciting ,and evaluating bids against established criteria, then awarding contracts through a transparent, auditable process that makes competitively negotiated pricing available to more than 50,000 government, education and nonprofit organizations across the US and Canada.

In practice, that means your local government fleets can leverage Sourcewell to quickly adapt to pressing needs in a way that doesn’t bypass the bidding process (which would be illegal), but which effectively says, “we trust Sourcewell’s process.”

raw_title: 10 Of The Most Influential Concept Cars Ever Made
title: 10 Of The Most Influential Concept Cars Ever Made
raw_summary: What is a concept car? The technical definition describes it as a single model built by an automaker to explore new engineering or design ideas. But with the current state of affairs, most concept cars seem more like PR stunts built to slip into people's algorithms. Take the color-shifting BMW I Vision Dee as an example. Is its E-Ink-covered body cool? Absolutely. Will we ever see this tech in a production car? Probably not. Some automakers use concepts to preview an upcoming model. The cute and cheerful Citroën 2CV Concept will surely result in an inexpensive production EV. That's great, but there's nothing really revolutionary in these concepts. These concepts don't often become the new gold standard for the company behind them, and other automakers aren't incensed to rush and replicate the design or technology of them. Sometimes, though, a concept car introduces a brand-new idea that then gets widespread, making it truly influential.

article_paragraphs: What is a concept car? The technical definition describes it as a single model built by an automaker to explore new engineering or design ideas. But with the current state of affairs, most concept cars seem more like PR stunts built to slip into people's algorithms. Take the color-shifting BMW I Vision Dee as an example. Is its E-Ink-covered body cool? Absolutely. Will we ever see this tech in a production car? Probably not.

Some automakers use concepts to preview an upcoming model. The cute and cheerful Citroën 2CV Concept will surely result in an inexpensive production EV. That's great, but there's nothing really revolutionary in these concepts. These concepts don't often become the new gold standard for the company behind them, and other automakers aren't incensed to rush and replicate the design or technology of them. Sometimes, though, a concept car introduces a brand-new idea that then gets widespread, making it truly influential.

Some concepts introduce a new design direction or invent a new vehicle category, while others showcase advanced tech that now we take for granted. In this piece, we'll have a closer look at many of those influential concepts. These cars all had major impacts on the industry, from the Buick Y-Job — the world's first concept car — to the GM Autonomy Concept, which introduced the skateboard chassis used in most modern EVs.

Before Harley Earl (one of the world's most famous designers ) showcased the first concept car, automakers mainly worked with coachbuilders to produce one-off cars for wealthy customers. The Y-Job, however, was never listed for sale. Instead, GM notes that Earl used it to demonstrate how a "Car of the Future" might look like.

The result was nothing short of a masterpiece. It might not be immediately obvious from a modern-day standpoint, but the Y-Job looks way sleeker and more elegant than other cars of its era. Earl achieved this thanks to longer and wider proportions to accentuate the car's stance – a design approach that's arguably followed to this day, particularly in coupes and sedans. There were other styling techniques from the Y-Job that other automakers implemented later, like hidden headlights, flush door handles, and integrated taillights.

The standout feature, though, was the intricate retractable roof that stayed hidden under the rear metal deck for a sleek topless look. Once opened, it uncovered a tech-forward interior with a top-mounted radio and electric windows. Adding to the futuristic experience, the Buick Y-Job also features a three-speed automatic transmission, two years before GM took the technology mainstream with the Hydra-Matic. The real kicker is that the Y-Job was a fully-functioning car powered by a 5.2-liter inline-eight engine with 141 horsepower. In fact, Harley Earl drove the Y-Job daily, as he thought the best way to showcase its design and technology was on the street — not in showrooms.

While they could certainly pass as Batmobiles, the B.A.T. designation of Alfa Romeo's 1950 concepts actually means "Berlinetta Aerodinamica Tecnica." Penned by legendary designer and aeronautic engineer Franco Scaglione, the B.A.T. concepts were designed with one idea in mind: cheating the wind. Showcased in 1953 at the Turin Motor Show, the B.A.T. 5 was the first of the trio. Based on the Alfa Romeo 1900 SS sedan, the concept featured a striking body. It had a pointy front end, convex windshield, and streamlined sides with covered front and rear wheels to minimize turbulence, while a big vent behind the front wheels discharged air from under the hood.

Still, it's the three rear fins that catch the most attention. They weren't styling gimmicks; instead, Scaglione used them to smooth out the airflow and allow it to converge at a single trailing point behind the car. By doing this, he has virtually elongated the car's body without using a tapered rear end. As a result, the B.A.T. 5 had a drag coefficient of 0.23 Cd and a top speed of over 124 mph. The B.A.T. 7 brought the former figure down to whopping 0.19 thanks to even more extreme wings, while the B.A.T. 9 was a simpler, more production-ready design.

raw_title: How To Tell Your Car's Oil Pump Is Going Bad
title: How To Tell Your Car's Oil Pump Is Going Bad
raw_summary: A car's oil pump plays a critical role in keeping the engine running smoothly. The pump circulates pressurized engine oil through the vehicle's lubrication system, sustaining critical components such as the crankshaft, camshaft, bearings, and valve train. The oil reduces friction between moving parts, limits wear, and helps carry a significant amount of heat away from the components it lubricates. If the pump fails to maintain adequate oil pressure, the engine can suffer severe damage, potentially requiring an expensive repair or even replacement. Oil pumps are designed to last for years, and many can operate for over 100,000 miles with proper maintenance. That said, wear and tear, contaminated oil, sludge accumulation, and prolonged maintenance can affect an oil pump's performance.
